metaDescription: Own coal, coalbed methane, or oil and gas minerals near Birmingham, AL? Get a hedged, activity-based cash offer confirmed against county probate records.
heroLead: Birmingham was built on Red Mountain iron ore and the coal seams of the Warrior field, and that history is precisely why so many Jefferson County families discover a mineral interest buried in an old estate file decades after the mines themselves went quiet.
intro: Iron, coal, and limestone drew industry to Birmingham in the late 1800s, and the mineral acquisitions that followed were sweeping, sometimes covering entire sections of land bought or leased from farm families for a fraction of what the minerals would later be worth. When the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane boom arrived in the 1980s, some of those same old coal reservations became gas assets, and heirs who had never thought about mineral rights suddenly had a royalty check to explain, or a lease offer to weigh, or, more often, neither.

We buy mineral and royalty interests from Birmingham-area owners at every stage: fresh inheritances just discovered in a probate file, older interests with a documented royalty history, and non-participating interests where the owner never had leasing rights at all.

sections.heading: Layers of mineral history under Jefferson County
paragraphs: It's routine for a Birmingham-area mineral title to show more than one severance: an original coal or iron reservation from a mining company a century ago, followed by a later coalbed methane lease covering the same coal seams for gas rather than solid mineral extraction. Untangling which company, estate, or family holds which layer is often the real work before an offer can be made.

Jefferson County's probate court, which sits in Birmingham itself, is the practical starting point for that work. Between deed records, wills, and prior lease filings, most ownership questions here can be traced, even when the current owner's only clue is an old royalty check or a line on a property tax bill.

sections.heading: Where CBM activity concentrated relative to the city
paragraphs: The Black Warrior Basin's most productive coalbed methane fields, including Oak Grove, Cedar Cove, and the broader Brookwood trend, sit primarily southwest of Birmingham toward Tuscaloosa County, with Jefferson County itself hosting a mix of core and flank acreage depending on the specific area. A tract closer to the city's urban core is typically valued differently than one in Jefferson County's less-developed southwestern reaches.

We check current well control and permit activity against the specific location of a Birmingham-area tract before quoting anything, since blanket citywide numbers don't hold up well against how uneven CBM development actually was across the county.

sections.heading: Heirs, estates, and small fractional interests
paragraphs: A large share of Birmingham mineral interests today are small fractional shares, the result of an original reservation dividing among children, then grandchildren, over three or four generations. It's common for a single heir to hold something like a sixteenth or thirty-second interest, often without realizing any co-owners exist elsewhere.

We buy interests at that scale regularly. Once your fractional share is confirmed against the county's probate and deed records, we quote a range built for that specific percentage rather than requiring you to first coordinate with every other heir.

sections.heading: What determines value on a Birmingham-area interest
paragraphs: For coalbed methane interests, we look at whether a well is currently producing on the relevant unit, how that well's output has trended, and how comparable interests in the surrounding field have recently sold or leased. For interests with no production history, the range is built from lease bonus comparables and permit activity in the surrounding area instead.

We won't quote a flat per-acre number sight unseen, and any figure we do give is hedged against current activity, since Black Warrior CBM production has declined meaningfully from its 1990s peak and continues to shift with commodity prices.

faqs.question: I found an old royalty statement in my grandparents' papers but haven't received anything in years. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It likely means the well that generated those payments has slowed or stopped producing, which is common as Black Warrior CBM wells age. We can check the current status of that specific well and quote based on where things stand today.

faqs.question: How do I find out if I'm one of several heirs to a Birmingham mineral interest?
faqs.answer: Jefferson County probate records usually show how an interest was divided among heirs over time. We help trace that history and confirm your specific share as part of the offer process.

faqs.question: Is my interest coal, coalbed methane, or oil and gas, and does it matter?
faqs.answer: It can matter quite a bit, since a coal reservation and a later gas lease on the same seam are sometimes held by different owners. We review the deed language and lease history to confirm exactly what you hold before quoting.

faqs.question: Do you buy interests with no current production?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many Birmingham-area interests we buy have no active well at all, and we price those against lease and permit comparables in the surrounding trend rather than a production record.

faqs.question: What's the difference between selling my mineral rights and leasing them?
faqs.answer: A lease is a temporary right to explore and produce in exchange for royalties if a company succeeds; selling transfers the mineral ownership itself for a lump sum now. We're glad to walk through the tradeoff.
